title: Beta kickoff: Dedicated staged rollouts (reserved pool) — Redwood x Northwind Health
summary: CS-led beta kickoff for Dedicated staged rollouts on Northwind’s reserved GPU pool. Redwood walked through staged rollout concepts (multi-stage traffic weights, gates, approvals), default gate metrics (p95 latency, 5xx/timeouts, queue depth, GPU utilization), and how failures/missing metrics pause rather than advance. Discussed audit logging needs (who approved, what changed, when) and export expectations for compliance. Aligned on onboarding steps: enable tenant allowlist flag, create first RolloutPlan, agree on stage recipe, validate dashboards, run a low-risk canary during a maintenance window, and define escalation paths for holds/rollbacks.
topics: Why Dedicated rollouts are riskier (reserved pool saturation, queuing, SLA impact)
Staged rollout model: stages, deterministic traffic allocation, evaluation windows
Gates: default thresholds, missing/late metrics behavior (fail-safe hold)
Manual approvals vs auto-advance, and who can approve (RBAC)
Audit events and export (compliance / change management)
Onboarding plan: feature flag, plan creation, first canary, support + oncall path
action_items: Rachel Kim: Send beta onboarding packet (enablement steps, known limitations, escalation path) to Northwind by 2025-01-16
Dev Patel: Confirm support escalation routing + after-hours oncall contact for beta rollout holds by 2025-01-17
Mark Feldman (Northwind): Share target SLOs and current alert thresholds for p95 latency, 5xx, and queue depth by 2025-01-20
Jenna Wu (Northwind): Provide audit log export requirements (fields/retention/SIEM format) by 2025-01-20
Omar Rahim (Northwind): Identify one low-risk model/config change to use as first staged rollout test by 2025-01-21
next_steps: Redwood to enable Dedicated staged rollouts feature flag for Northwind’s tenant and reserved pool (beta allowlist).
30-min follow-up to review proposed stage plan and gate defaults (5% → 25% → 100%, with manual approvals).
Schedule first canary in Northwind’s change window; Redwood to monitor gate dashboards live and agree on rollback criteria.
Security follow-up if needed on audit event schema + export timing.
transcript:
Meeting: Beta kickoff: Dedicated staged rollouts (reserved pool) — Redwood x Northwind Health
Recorded by Fireflies.ai
Date: 2025-01-14
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 46 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS), Miguel Santos (Enterprise CS), Dev Patel (Support Escalations)
Northwind Health: Priya Desai (Platform Eng Manager), Mark Feldman (SRE Lead), Jenna Wu (Security/Compliance), Omar Rahim (ML Platform Eng)

---
Summary (auto)
- Discussed Dedicated staged rollouts beta, traffic splitting, gates, approvals, and audit logging.
- Agreed on onboarding steps and success criteria for first rollout.

Action items (auto)
- Redwood to send onboarding docs and confirm feature flag enablement.
- Northwind to share SLO thresholds and audit logging requirements.

---

[00:00] Rachel Kim: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the beta kickoff for staged rollouts for Dedicated pools. I’m Rachel, I run enterprise customer success on this account. Miguel’s here with me and Dev from Support, mainly because we want to make sure escalation and the “what if it pauses at 2 AM” stuff is very clear.

[00:17] Priya Desai: Sounds good. Yeah, thanks Rachel. We’ve been waiting for this one.

[00:21] Mark Feldman: Yep.

[00:22] Jenna Wu: Hi.

[00:23] Omar Rahim: Hey.

[00:25] Rachel Kim: Great. So, agenda: (1) why we built this specifically for Dedicated, (2) what the staged rollout object looks like in practice—stages, gates, approvals, (3) onboarding steps for beta, and then we’ll close on success criteria and next meeting.

[00:42] Miguel Santos: And we’ll also cover limitations. It’s beta, so we want to be explicit about what’s in and what’s not.

[00:49] Rachel Kim: Priya, do you want to give the 60-second recap of what’s been painful for you so we anchor on the right problems?

[00:56] Priya Desai: Yeah. Today, when we update a model version or even like a runtime config change, it’s basically pool-wide. And since it’s reserved capacity, if the new thing is slower or starts throwing timeouts, the queue depth climbs immediately. We had one incident last quarter where we had to do a manual revert and it still took… what was it, like 20 minutes for the queue to drain.

[01:18] Mark Feldman: Closer to 30, because the retry storm kicked in.

[01:21] Priya Desai: Right, yeah. And we’re trying to get to a standard change management flow where we can prove approvals and an audit trail. Right now it’s like… screenshots and Slack threads.

[01:33] Jenna Wu: And from compliance side, we need “who approved what change and when” plus retention. Even if it’s not SOX, it’s basically SOC2 controls for change management.

[01:42] Rachel Kim: Yep, that tracks exactly with why this project exists. Dedicated is uniquely risky because you don’t have infinite capacity to absorb a regression. Hosted has more routing escape hatches; Dedicated is “this is your pool,” and so blast radius is your pool.

[01:57] Dev Patel: Also the operational issue is the manual steps can differ by operator. In beta, we’re trying to reduce those foot-guns.

[02:05] Rachel Kim: Okay, so what is staged rollout? The mental model: you create a Rollout Plan on a specific Dedicated pool and route. That plan has stages. Each stage has a traffic weight, like 5% of traffic to the candidate version, and the rest stays on baseline. Then each stage has gates, which are basically checks over metrics over a time window. If the gates pass, you can advance to the next stage either manually (approval) or automatic (auto-advance) depending on policy.

[02:33] Omar Rahim: Is it like… we can do 5% to new model and 95% to old model, but on the same pool? That’s the part I wasn’t sure about because we’re reserved.

[02:42] Miguel Santos: Good question. Yes, but it’s “same pool” in the sense of same reserved pool boundary, not mixing tenants. Internally we carve the pool into allocations, and routing decides which requests go to baseline vs candidate. The important part: we’re not borrowing capacity from other tenants, and we’re not pushing your traffic to a hosted shared fleet.

[03:02] Mark Feldman: So it still shares the GPU inventory though. Like if the candidate is slower, it can still affect baseline latency, right?

[03:10] Rachel Kim: Exactly. That’s why the gates include queue depth and utilization in addition to just error rate, because a candidate can “look fine” but still cause saturation.

[03:21] Priya Desai: And is traffic assignment deterministic? We’ve had issues in other systems where it’s random per request and then debugging is annoying.

[03:29] Miguel Santos: It’s deterministic hashing. So, same request key—typically conversation_id or a stable request id—maps consistently. If you don’t have a stable key, we can fall back to request id but then it’s basically random.

[03:42] Omar Rahim: We do have conversation IDs for chat. For embeddings, not really.

[03:47] Miguel Santos: For embeddings, we can use a client-provided idempotency key if you already send one. We’ll go through recommended keys in onboarding.

[03:55] Rachel Kim: Let’s talk about gates. In beta, the default gate pack we recommend for Dedicated is:
- p95 latency threshold (route-level)
- 5xx rate and/or timeout rate
- queue depth max (or “queue depth slope” in some setups)
- GPU utilization ceiling / headroom check
And there’s also a “metrics freshness” check.

[04:18] Jenna Wu: Can you say more about “freshness”? Like you pause if metrics are missing?

[04:23] Rachel Kim: Yes. This is one of the more conservative behaviors: if we can’t evaluate a gate because metrics are late or missing, we fail safe by holding the rollout. We do not advance stages if the evaluator is degraded.

[04:37] Mark Feldman: That’s good. We prefer hold over “blindly proceed.”

[04:41] Priya Desai: But what about false positives? Like if Prometheus is lagging for a minute, it pauses everything?

[04:47] Miguel Santos: There’s a tolerance window. We look at an evaluation window (say 10 minutes) and require data points within the last N minutes. If not, we mark the gate as “unknown” and hold. You’ll see that explicitly in the UI as “Missing metrics” instead of “Failed.”

[05:05] Dev Patel: From ops perspective, that distinction matters, because the runbook is different: missing metrics means investigate telemetry pipeline first, not roll back the model.

[05:14] Rachel Kim: Exactly. In beta, we want you to treat “unknown” as stop-the-line, then decide: proceed manually, or wait, or abort.

[05:23] Omar Rahim: Abort equals rollback to baseline?

[05:26] Miguel Santos: Abort means stop sending traffic to candidate and return to baseline routing weights. It also ends the plan run, but preserves the audit trail.

[05:36] Priya Desai: So there’s baseline vs candidate versions. How do we define the candidate? Is it model version, runtime version, config, all of that?

[05:44] Rachel Kim: In v1, the rollout “target” is a deployment spec: model version + runtime config bundle. So it can represent model weights change, quantization profile change, batching config changes, whatever. That’s intentional because many regressions come from “small” config changes.

[06:02] Mark Feldman: Great.

[06:04] Rachel Kim: Approvals: the policy we recommend for your account is manual approvals at each stage. So stage 1 (5%) runs for 15 minutes, gates pass, then it pauses waiting for a human approval to go to 25%. Same between 25% and 100%. You can also set an auto-advance, but given you’re in regulated healthcare, we’re assuming manual.

[06:25] Jenna Wu: Yes, manual approval is required for us. Also, we need to control who can approve.

[06:31] Miguel Santos: That’s RBAC. In beta, we’re enabling it for Redwood operators and your enterprise admin role. We’ll align with your SSO groups. It’s not “anyone with console access.”

[06:44] Priya Desai: We use Okta groups, mapped to roles.

[06:47] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[06:49] Jenna Wu: And audit logs—do we get events? Like “Priya approved stage 2” and timestamps?

[06:56] Rachel Kim: Yes. The audit events include actor, tenant, pool id, rollout plan id, plan version, stage id, action (create/update/approve/abort/auto-hold). And timestamps. For beta, you’ll see them in Redwood Console audit log view, and we can also export via your existing audit export pipeline.

[07:16] Jenna Wu: Export as… what format? We ingest JSON into Splunk.

[07:20] Dev Patel: It’s structured JSON. We can provide an example payload. There’s also a CSV export in Console but the better path is the event stream.

[07:29] Mark Feldman: Is retention configurable? We need at least 1 year.

[07:33] Rachel Kim: For Dedicated enterprise, yes, we support 400 days in our standard compliance retention tier. We can confirm your contract line item, but functionally it’s available.

[07:44] Priya Desai: Okay.

[07:46] Rachel Kim: Let’s walk through a concrete example plan, and you can tell me if it matches how you’d do change windows.
Stage 0: optional shadow/internal validation. For Dedicated, shadow is a little tricky because it’s additional load; we can do mirrored requests in a limited way, but it’s not enabled by default.
Stage 1: 5% to candidate, 95% baseline, evaluation window 10 minutes, manual approval required.
Stage 2: 25% candidate, 75% baseline, evaluation window 15 minutes, manual approval.
Stage 3: 100% candidate, finalize.

[08:23] Mark Feldman: I like that. I’d maybe make stage 1 longer, like 20 minutes, depending on traffic. But conceptually yes.

[08:30] Omar Rahim: For our traffic, nights are low. Doing it at night makes gates noisy.

[08:35] Priya Desai: We do change windows Tuesday 1–3 PM Eastern. That’s when traffic is moderate.

[08:42] Rachel Kim: Great, that’s actually ideal for gating.

[08:45] Miguel Santos: On the gate defaults, we’ll propose thresholds, but we want your SRE thresholds. For example, p95 latency: we can set absolute (like p95 < 900ms) or relative (like not more than +15% over baseline). Relative is often more portable.

[09:03] Mark Feldman: Relative is better because our baseline can shift if we change prompts.

[09:08] Rachel Kim: Yep. Same for 5xx: we can do “5xx rate < 0.2%” and “timeout rate < 0.1%,” but if your baseline is 0.01% then you might want tighter.

[09:22] Jenna Wu: Are these gates per route? We have like three critical routes.

[09:27] Miguel Santos: Per route within the pool. In the UI you’ll attach the plan to a pool + route, and gates evaluate on that. We’re intentionally not doing “global tenant metrics” because cardinality and because it hides which workload is failing.

[09:43] Priya Desai: That’s good.

[09:45] Omar Rahim: What about quality gates? Like, we run offline evals, but not in real time.

[09:51] Rachel Kim: In v1, quality is optional and mostly manual. Some customers plug in a custom signal, but we’re not promising per-request semantic gating. If you have a simple proxy signal (like tool-call success rate), we can discuss. But for beta we’re focusing on reliability + capacity gates.

[10:11] Mark Feldman: Makes sense.

[10:13] Rachel Kim: Failure behavior: if a gate fails, the plan will automatically go to “Hold” and stop stage advancement. Depending on the gate, we can also recommend auto-rollback, but by default in your setup it will hold and require a human to abort or proceed.

[10:31] Mark Feldman: I prefer hold. Auto rollback is okay but we need to review.

[10:35] Priya Desai: Agree.

[10:37] Dev Patel: In practice, if you see queue depth spiking, you will probably choose abort. But the system won’t do it unless you tell it to, in your policy.

[10:47] Jenna Wu: If it holds, do we get notifications?

[10:50] Miguel Santos: Yes, there are alerts we can configure: “rollout paused” and “gate evaluator lag.” For beta, Redwood can also set up a webhook to your PagerDuty or Slack.

[11:03] Mark Feldman: PagerDuty please. We’ll give you an integration key.

[11:07] Rachel Kim: Great.

[11:09] Priya Desai: Quick question—does traffic split respect sticky sessions? Like chat sessions.

[11:14] Miguel Santos: Yes if you provide the key. Otherwise we do best-effort. The important part is: for a conversation, we don’t want to flip between baseline and candidate mid-conversation.

[11:27] Omar Rahim: We can pass conversation_id. Cool.

[11:30] Rachel Kim: Onboarding steps for beta:
1) Redwood enables the feature flag for your tenant and pool. This is an allowlist.
2) We provision roles: who can create/edit vs who can approve/abort.
3) You create a first rollout plan in Console (or via API if you prefer). For beta, we recommend Console so you can see gate statuses.
4) We validate dashboards: latency, error rate, queue depth, utilization. There’s a “rollout health” dashboard too.
5) Run a test rollout with a low-risk change (like runtime minor version or a non-critical route) during your change window.
6) Post-run review: did gates behave as expected, any false holds, did audit logs export correctly.

[12:17] Mark Feldman: That sounds fine.

[12:19] Jenna Wu: The export correctness is important. We also need to validate the fields match our policies.

[12:25] Dev Patel: We can do a dry run: create plan, approve stage, abort—just to generate events without actually changing a model. But note it still touches routing, so we’d do it on a non-critical route first.

[12:39] Priya Desai: We have an internal-only route that’s fine.

[12:41] Rachel Kim: Perfect.

[12:43] Omar Rahim: For the “candidate” deployment, do we need to pre-warm anything? We’ve seen cold start behaviors.

[12:50] Miguel Santos: Dedicated pool doesn’t cold start in the same way as serverless, but you can still have cache warmup effects. In beta, we recommend a warmup step: send synthetic traffic to candidate at 0% public traffic, if possible, or start at 1% for a short period. The stage system supports 1%.

[13:10] Mark Feldman: That would help. We can generate synthetic load.

[13:13] Rachel Kim: Great.

[13:15] Priya Desai: Can you explain the autoscaling guardrail? Because we’re reserved, but we do have some burst nodes sometimes.

[13:22] Miguel Santos: Right. Your dedicated pool can have a burst policy. During a rollout, we enforce headroom rules so that stage changes don’t accidentally eat all headroom. For example, if GPU util is already above 80%, we might block moving from 25% to 100% until it drops. That’s part of the gating system.

[13:43] Mark Feldman: Okay, so that’s a gate.

[13:45] Miguel Santos: Essentially yes, a capacity gate.

[13:48] Jenna Wu: And who can override that? Like, can we force it?

[13:52] Rachel Kim: You can override with manual approval, but it will be auditable. And we’d recommend not overriding unless you’ve mitigated the cause.

[14:03] Mark Feldman: Yeah, we probably won’t override.

[14:06] Priya Desai: Another question: is it per-pool only? We have two pools in two regions.

[14:13] Miguel Santos: In beta, it’s per pool. You can run two separate plans. Cross-region coordinated rollout is a roadmap item.

[14:22] Priya Desai: Okay.

[14:24] Rachel Kim: That’s one of the beta limitations: no “one plan controlling multiple pools.” But we can help with a playbook: do us-east first, then eu-west, etc.

[14:36] Omar Rahim: How does rollback work? If stage 2 fails, do we go back to stage 1 automatically?

[14:41] Miguel Santos: Not automatically. It holds. You can either abort to baseline (0% candidate) or you can reduce weight manually, but the typical action is abort. “Rollback to previous stage” is something we’re considering but not in beta.

[14:57] Mark Feldman: Abort is fine.

[15:00] Rachel Kim: I want to check success criteria for you. For us, success is: you run at least one staged rollout without incident, gates reflect your reality, and you get an audit trail that Jenna can sign off on. Is that aligned?

[15:15] Jenna Wu: Yes. I also want to confirm retention and export.

[15:19] Priya Desai: And I want a predictable operator workflow. Like, my team can own it, not Redwood.

[15:25] Rachel Kim: In beta, Redwood will still be very involved, but yes the UI and process is built for you to own it.

[15:33] Dev Patel: And support-wise, we want to confirm the escalation: if a rollout pauses due to “missing metrics,” you’ll see it, you’ll page us, we’ll triage whether it’s metrics pipeline vs actual regression.

[15:46] Mark Feldman: Makes sense.

[15:48] Rachel Kim: Can I ask, are you evaluating other options for rollouts? Sometimes folks mention AWS Bedrock or just self-hosting.

[15:56] Priya Desai: We looked at Bedrock for some non-PHI workloads, but for this dedicated pool, we’re committed to Redwood. The issue is mostly change management.

[16:06] Mark Feldman: Yeah, we don’t want to rebuild routing and gating ourselves.

[16:10] Rachel Kim: Good.

[16:12] Jenna Wu: We also use OpenAI for a separate workflow, but we can’t use it for our regulated workloads.

[16:18] Rachel Kim: Understood.

[16:20] Miguel Santos: One more detail: you’ll see “plan versions.” If you edit a plan mid-flight, it creates a new version and the audit logs reflect that. This helps with “what changed” tracking.

[16:33] Priya Desai: So you can’t silently edit.

[16:35] Miguel Santos: Exactly.

[16:37] Omar Rahim: Does API support idempotency? Like if our automation retries.

[16:42] Miguel Santos: Yes, create/update endpoints support idempotency keys. Approve/abort are also idempotent. There was a race condition earlier in internal testing; we fixed it. In beta we still recommend doing approves through Console initially.

[17:00] Priya Desai: Okay.

[17:01] Mark Feldman: Metrics—what’s the source? Is it your telemetry pipeline or can it read ours?

[17:07] Miguel Santos: It reads Redwood’s telemetry, because we need consistent tags and low-cardinality. You can correlate with yours, but the gates are based on our data.

[17:19] Mark Feldman: And what’s the evaluation frequency?

[17:22] Miguel Santos: Default is every 60 seconds. Windowing is like 10 minutes, but evaluated each minute.

[17:31] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[17:32] Rachel Kim: Can we talk about the first change you want to test with? Omar, any ideas?

[17:38] Omar Rahim: We have a minor change: updating the batching parameters for our summarization route. It’s not critical like triage chat, but it’s enough to test latency and queue depth.

[17:51] Mark Feldman: That one can still hurt if it slows down, but it’s manageable.

[17:55] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[17:57] Rachel Kim: Great candidate.

[18:00] Jenna Wu: For audit logs, can we get a sample now? Like, are you able to share a schema doc.

[18:05] Dev Patel: We can share an example payload after. It includes fields like actor_email, actor_role, action, resource_id, previous_value hash, new_value hash. Some of those fields might be labeled slightly differently; I’ll send the exact.

[18:23] Jenna Wu: Great.

[18:25] Rachel Kim: Also, approvals: we can configure “two-person rule” in the future. In beta it’s single approver, but we can require the approver role is separate from editor.

[18:37] Jenna Wu: That’s acceptable for beta. Longer term we’ll want two-person approvals.

[18:44] Priya Desai: Yeah, editor vs approver separation is good.

[18:48] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[18:50] Mark Feldman: How do you display gate status? I’m thinking my oncall will need to understand quickly.

[18:56] Miguel Santos: In Console, stage list shows gate badges: Pass / Fail / Unknown. Clicking in shows details: metric, threshold, current value, window, last datapoint timestamp. There’s also “why held” summary.

[19:14] Mark Feldman: Unknown is missing metrics.

[19:16] Miguel Santos: Exactly.

[19:18] Dev Patel: And there’s a link to the dashboard panel pre-filtered for that pool + route, so you can jump to graphs.

[19:26] Mark Feldman: Nice.

[19:27] Priya Desai: Is there a CLI? Some of our stuff is automated.

[19:32] Miguel Santos: There’s an internal CLI for Redwood operators. For customers, API is the supported path. But in beta we can share sample curl or a small script.

[19:44] Priya Desai: Okay.

[19:46] Rachel Kim: Let’s align on timeline. If we enable the feature flag this week, could we run the first test next Tuesday in your change window?

[19:56] Priya Desai: Next Tuesday works.

[19:58] Mark Feldman: Yeah, but we need to finalize thresholds before then.

[20:02] Rachel Kim: Right. Mark, if you can send current SLO and alert thresholds by end of week, Paula—sorry, not on this call—our product lead can propose defaults, and we’ll review in a 30-min session.

[20:16] Mark Feldman: I can send by Monday.

[20:18] Rachel Kim: Perfect.

[20:20] Jenna Wu: I’ll send audit log requirements too.

[20:23] Rachel Kim: Great.

[20:25] Omar Rahim: What about “shadow stage”? You said it’s tricky.

[20:28] Miguel Santos: Yeah, shadow means duplicating traffic, which increases load on the pool. On reserved pools, we’re cautious. A safer alternative is “1% stage with warmup” and maybe synthetic traffic. That keeps load bounded.

[20:45] Omar Rahim: Got it.

[20:47] Mark Feldman: And if we do 5% but traffic is low, is that enough sample size?

[20:52] Miguel Santos: The gate evaluation is time-window based, so if request volume is too low, the statistics can be noisy. In those cases, we recommend longer windows or higher initial weight, but only if headroom is good.

[21:08] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[21:10] Rachel Kim: Also, we can gate on absolute counts, like “at least N requests” before evaluating, but again beta scope is limited. We can tune windows instead.

[21:22] Priya Desai: Longer window is fine.

[21:25] Dev Patel: Just keep in mind longer windows mean slower time to detect. So we want the right balance.

[21:33] Mark Feldman: Yeah.

[21:35] Rachel Kim: Any other questions on mechanics?

[21:38] Jenna Wu: One more: do we get a report at the end? Like a PDF or something.

[21:43] Rachel Kim: Not a PDF, but the rollout run has a summary view: start/end, stages, approvals, gate results. You can export as JSON or CSV from Console. And all events are in the audit log.

[21:58] Jenna Wu: Okay.

[22:00] Priya Desai: Do you support maintenance mode? Like we pause traffic shift.

[22:05] Miguel Santos: You can pause the rollout at any stage. There’s a “Pause” action separate from “Hold due to gate.”

[22:12] Priya Desai: Good.

[22:14] Mark Feldman: For rollback, abort is immediate?

[22:17] Miguel Santos: Routing weight change is immediate, but draining in-flight requests still takes a bit. But you should see queue depth start to recover quickly.

[22:28] Mark Feldman: Okay.

[22:30] Rachel Kim: Let’s do a quick recap of responsibilities. Redwood: enable feature flag, set up RBAC mapping, share docs, set up alerts. Northwind: provide thresholds and audit requirements, pick first change, provide PagerDuty integration. Did I miss anything?

[22:48] Priya Desai: That covers it.

[22:50] Omar Rahim: All good.

[22:52] Jenna Wu: Yep.

[22:53] Mark Feldman: Yep.

[22:55] Rachel Kim: Cool. Dev, anything from support side?

[22:58] Dev Patel: Just one ask: when we do the first rollout, please have an oncall reachable on your side for the full window. If it pauses, we might need quick decision: proceed vs abort. We can’t decide that for you.

[23:11] Priya Desai: Yes, we’ll have someone.

[23:13] Mark Feldman: I’ll be there.

[23:15] Rachel Kim: Great.

[23:17] Miguel Santos: One last thing: for deterministic routing, make sure your client sends the conversation_id header consistently. I’ll send the exact field name; I think you already pass something similar.

[23:29] Omar Rahim: Okay, send it, I’ll verify.

[23:32] Rachel Kim: Awesome. We’ll send the onboarding packet by Thursday and propose a 30-min thresholds review Friday or Monday. Anything else?

[23:43] Jenna Wu: Nothing else.

[23:45] Priya Desai: Thanks everyone.

[23:47] Rachel Kim: Thanks all. Talk soon.

---
Notes
- Some crosstalk and minor transcription errors present.
- Follow-up meeting to be scheduled for gate thresholds and plan review.
